title: Electric Field and Electric Field Intensity
short_intro: The electric field is a vector space property surrounding a source charge that exerts a force on any other test charge placed within it. It is defined quantitatively as the electrostatic force experienced per unit positive test charge.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Calculation of electric field due to point charges, discrete charge distributions, linear, surface, and volume charge distributions, and basic superposition principle.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Continuous charge distributions, Gauss's law applications for symmetric charge systems (spherical, cylindrical, planar), and differential form of Gauss's law.

prerequisites: Integration techniques for continuous charge distributions

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Physical Significance
bullets: Electric field intensity (E) at a point is the limit of the ratio of electrostatic force (F) to a vanishingly small positive test charge (q_0).
It is measured in Newtons per Coulomb (N/C) or Volts per meter (V/m), with dimensions [M L T^-3 A^-1].
The electric field acts as a mediator for electrostatic interactions, traveling at the speed of light in vacuum.

concept_notes.heading: Electric Field Lines
bullets: Imaginary lines drawn to represent the direction and magnitude of the electric field in space.
They originate on positive charges and terminate on negative charges, never forming closed loops.
The tangent to a field line at any point gives the direction of the electric field vector at that point, and their relative density represents field magnitude.

concept_notes.heading: Superposition Principle for Electric Field
bullets: The net electric field at a point due to a system of discrete charges is the vector sum of the electric fields produced by each individual charge.
E_net = E_1 + E_2 + ... + E_n = sum over i of E_i.
This principle holds because Maxwell's equations and Coulomb's law are linear.

concept_notes.heading: Gauss's Law and Symmetry
bullets: Relates the total electric flux passing through a closed hypothetical surface (Gaussian surface) to the net charge enclosed by that surface.
Expressed mathematically as the surface integral of E dot dA equals q_enclosed divided by epsilon_0.
Simplifies the calculation of electric fields for highly symmetric charge distributions like spherical, cylindrical, and planar geometries.

derivations.title: Electric Field due to a Point Charge
derivations.conditions: A stationary point charge q in vacuum or free space.
steps: Place a test charge q_0 at a distance r from the source charge q.
Apply Coulomb's law to find the force between the charges: F = \frac{1}{4piepsilon_0} \frac{q q_0}{r^2} \hat{r}.
Use the definition of electric field E = \frac{F}{q_0}.
Substitute the force equation into the definition to cancel q_0.

derivations.title: Electric Field due to an Infinite Thin Plane Sheet of Charge
derivations.conditions: Uniform surface charge density sigma on an infinite, non-conducting plane sheet.
steps: Construct a cylindrical Gaussian surface of cross-sectional area A penetrating perpendicularly through the sheet.
Evaluate the electric flux through the two flat end-caps of the cylinder: \Phi = 2 E A.
Calculate the total charge enclosed within the Gaussian surface: q_enclosed = \sigma A.
Apply Gauss's law: \Phi = \frac{q_enclosed}{\epsilon_0} \implies 2 E A = \frac{\sigma A}{\epsilon_0}.

graphs_and_experiments.title: E vs r Graph for a Point Charge
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A rectangular hyperbola curve showing E decreasing non-linearly as 1/r^2 with increasing distance r.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the inverse-square law relationship between electric field magnitude and distance from a point source.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in MCQs to identify correct graphical trends for Coulombic fields versus dipole fields (1/r^3).

graphs_and_experiments.title: E vs r Graph for a Solid Conducting Sphere
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: E = 0 from r = 0 up to r = R, followed by a sharp step-up at r = R, then falling off as 1/r^2 for r > R.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Reflects the physical principle that static electric field inside a conductor is zero and charge resides entirely on the surface.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in conceptual conceptual matching and numerical threshold questions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Millikan's Oil Drop Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic of an atomizer, viewing microscope, parallel capacitor plates, and ionizing X-ray source.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Measures the elementary electronic charge e by balancing gravitational force, buoyant force, viscous drag, and upward electric force (qE = mg).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Historical experiment questions regarding charge quantization and electric field balance.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the magnitude of the electric field at a distance of 20 cm from a point charge of 4 micro-C in vacuum.
solution_steps: Identify given values: q = 4 \times 10^{-6} C, r = 0.2 m, 1/(4\pi\epsilon_0) = 9 \times 10^9 N m^2/C^2.
Substitute values into the formula E = \frac{1}{4piepsilon_0} \frac{q}{r^2}.

solved_numericals.question: An infinite non-conducting sheet of charge has a uniform surface charge density of 17.7 micro-C/m^2. Calculate the electric field intensity near the sheet.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: \sigma = 17.7 \times 10^{-6} C/m^2, \epsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} C^2/(N m^2).
Use the formula for an infinite sheet: E = \frac{\sigma}{2epsilon_0}.

solved_numericals.question: A uniform electric field E = 3 x 10^3 i-hat N/C passes through a surface of area 10 m^2 parallel to the yz-plane. What is the electric flux through the surface?
solution_steps: Identify field vector E = 3 \times 10^3 \hat{i} N/C and area vector A = 10 \hat{i} m^2 (since surface is parallel to yz-plane, normal is along x-axis).
Apply definition of electric flux: \Phi = E \cdot A.

assumptions_and_limitations: Coulomb's law and standard electric field formulas assume stationary point charges (electrostatic regime), ignoring relativistic magnetic effects of moving charges.
Infinite sheet and line charge formulas are idealized approximations valid only when the distance from the edges is much smaller than the physical dimensions of the charged object.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Electric field lines physically exist as tangible threads in space.
common_misconceptions.correct: Electric field lines are merely a geometrical visualization tool to represent field direction and relative intensity.
common_misconceptions.why: They do not have a physical substance; space between them is continuous.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A test charge must always be positive and static.
common_misconceptions.correct: A test charge is an idealized mathematical point charge assumed to be infinitesimally small so it does not disturb the source charge distribution.
common_misconceptions.why: Its sign only determines the conventional direction of the force vector, but the field itself exists independently of the test charge.

quick_revision: Electric field direction is always along the tangent to the electric field line at any point.
Electric Field of a Point Charge: E = \frac{1}{4piepsilon_0} \frac{q}{r^2}
